group.passage:
Bedford, an American psychology professor, died of kidney cancer. At the end of his life, he expressed his desire to be cryogenically frozen. [[1]] Before he died, he paid $100,000 to have his body frozen after death. When he finally kicked the bucket on January 12, 1967, he became the first person to be cryogenically frozen after death.
The process of preserving Bedford’s body encountered its fair share of twists and turns. The science of cryonics was underdeveloped at that time. [[2]] After his sudden death, his nurse rushed to collect ice from neighbors to start cooling his body. Members from a group of cryonic enthusiasts gathered to pump oxygen into his veins in order to protect his brain. This team of “experts” packed his body in dry ice at -79°C and moved him into liquid nitrogen at -196°C at a facility in Phoenix, Arizona.
In 1982, Bedford’s body was entrusted to the Alcor Life Extension Foundation, a professional cryonics company. However, examinations revealed signs of damage resulting from the crude preservation process. The technology used on Bedford was primitive compared to modern techniques. His skin had cracked, his limbs were discolored, and his nose was flattened by the dry ice. [[3]] True vitrification, which prevents cell damage, wasn’t invented until the 1980s. The chemicals used likely ruined Bedford’s brain beyond repair.
Some scientists believe it is impossible to revive Bedford’s frozen body. Bedford remains frozen, not legally alive but not considered dead either. After Bedford, more than 300 people have joined in cryonic suspension at facilities around the world. [[4]] Bedford’s case, along with his counterparts, represents both the hopes and challenges of cryonics.

options_bank.A: If somehow revived, he would look ghostly.
options_bank.B: There were neither standard procedures nor enough equipment to preserve a body.
options_bank.C: He hoped that future technology would be able to repair his body and revive his consciousness.
options_bank.D: Even though science has improved, it remains uncertain whether those frozen bodies could ever be revived.

tags.topic: the first cryogenically frozen person and the challenges of cryonics
